title: Memory Decoder at Scale — where the paper and the code part ways
subtitle: Only the divergent steps are drawn. Each node states both sides; the lane says which stage of the pipeline the divergence sits in.
source: paper arXiv:2607.27919v1  ×  repo MemoryDecoder-at-Scale @ bbbfee85   ·   servers/memorydecoder/verification.md, 133 assertions checked (105 ✓ / 5 ✗ / 22 ◐ / 1 ?)
footer: memory-bench · methodology flow · paper ↔ code divergence
legend_notes: The single most consequential divergence: the paper's distributed OPQ+HNSW+sharded Faiss pipeline (the whole reason it can scale to 207B tokens) is a single-machine IndexIVFPQ in the open-source release — no OPQ, no HNSW, no sharding, and each process loads the FULL index onto its own GPU rather than searching a shard.

--ignore_first quietly changes the math: the paper's rule is 'drop the neighbor only if its key equals the query'; the code drops the top-1 neighbor unconditionally, so every trained checkpoint was distilled from K-1=1023 effective neighbors, not K=1024.

d7 is drawn in the A4 lane, not B2, on purpose: KNNWrapperMulti is a fully implemented classic online kNN-LM (retrieve + interpolate at inference) sitting in the repo with zero reachable call sites. If it were ever wired in it would populate B2 RECALL and B6 DELIVER — exactly the retrieval-at-inference mechanism the paper's central claim eliminates — but since it never executes, the coverage-matrix finding that B1-B5 are empty for the live system is unaffected.

λ selection is the other place documentation undersells the code: the paper describes one mechanism (validation-tuned, then fixed); the code has three independently written implementations, and two of them (FinEval's own launcher and the standalone knowledge scripts) both hardcode 0.3 while looking, at a glance, like they might share the registry that only the general suite actually uses.
